chapter_theme: The ten of பொய்ப் பத்து calls ten things false, each a state or wish of a person who lacks what it needs: good life for the wise man aside, the eminent without anger, the drinker without lapse, gain without timing, safety without foresight, rising without bearing one's lot, greatness without bearing lowliness and its mirror, justice from the greedy, and penance from the impure.
structure_note: Line 1 of 61 frames the whole ten. 61 alone turns the pattern round (a gift that rules out a bad life); 67 and 68 are a mirrored pair; the ten moves from the private faults of anger and drink to the king's justice and the ascetic's penance at its close.

61.reading: That a person of great understanding should fail to live well is called false.
61.nuance: Line 1 is the frame of the whole ten, so the saying of 61 is line 2 alone. Every saying of this ten has the shape 'for such a person, such a thing is a lie': a state or wish is denied to a type of person, and the ten works by naming what the person lacks or has. Here the denial runs the other way from the rest: great understanding rules out a bad life, where the other nine name a lack that rules out a good.

items.claim: a man of great understanding failing to live well is a falsehood, a thing that does not happen

62.reading: On the most direct reading of a doubtful line, that one of great eminence should be without anger is called false.
62.nuance: ஒன்றன் makes no clear sense as printed; the ten's pattern wants a person-noun (one of great eminence, perhaps பெருஞ்சீரோன் with தன்), and the reading assumes that. Read so, the line does not praise anger: it says the eminent are never in fact free of it, which may be a warning about the powerful rather than a licence. If ஒன்றன் is kept as 'of one thing', the sense cannot be fixed.

items.claim: a man of great eminence being without anger is a falsehood

63.reading: That a drinker of toddy should be free of lapses is called false.
63.nuance: சோர்வு is a slip or a letting go, of attention, of speech or of a secret; the line does not say drink makes a man wicked, only that it makes him unreliable.

items.claim: a toddy-drinker being free of lapses is a falsehood

64.reading: That one who does not know the right time should get what he aims at into his hand is called false.
64.nuance: கையுறல் is 'coming into the hand'; the failure the line names is not of effort or strength but of timing alone.

items.claim: success coming into the hand of one who does not know the time is a falsehood

65.reading: That one who does not know what is coming should be able to guard himself is called false.
65.nuance: மேல்வரவு is literally 'what comes upon one' or 'what comes later'; the line makes knowing it the condition of any self-protection, so guarding is first a matter of foresight, not of defences.

items.claim: self-protection by one who does not know what is coming is a falsehood

66.reading: That one who chafes against the work or trouble that falls to him should seek to rise is called false.
66.nuance: உறுவினை can be the task in hand or what one's past deeds bring upon one; காய்வோன் is one who resents or burns against it. On either reading the line ties rising to accepting what falls to one, but whether that is the labour of the work or the burden of fate the words do not settle.

items.claim: one who resents what falls to him wanting to rise is a falsehood

67.reading: That one who will not bear lowliness should seek greatness is called false.
67.nuance: நோனாதோன் is one who does not endure: the line makes the patient bearing of small estate the way to great estate, not its opposite.

items.claim: one who cannot bear lowliness wanting greatness is a falsehood

68.reading: That one who will not bear greatness should seek lowliness is called false, the exact mirror of 67.
68.nuance: The line swaps the two words of 67, and its sense is less plain. It may mean that one who cannot carry high station has no real choice of humility, since only the great can stoop by choice; or that one who cannot bear another's greatness wishes him low, and that wish is vain. The first keeps the ten's pattern of a wish denied by a lack; the second reads சிறுமை as the other's fall.

items.claim: one who cannot bear greatness choosing lowliness is a falsehood

69.reading: That one with a craving for wealth should do justice is called false.
69.domain_note: the king or anyone who sits in judgement
69.nuance: முறைசெயல் is the doing of justice, the king's or the judge's work; பொருள்நசை வேட்கை doubles the word for desire (நசை, வேட்கை), so the fault named is not having wealth but hunger for it.

items.claim: one who hungers for wealth doing justice is a falsehood

70.reading: That one who is not pure should perform penance is called false.
70.nuance: வாலியன் is the clean or pure one; the line does not say whether the purity is of mind or of body, but nothing in it points to a ritual rule, and in a ten about inner lacks it reads most naturally as purity of mind. The penance of the impure is not called useless but false, a show.

items.claim: penance done by one who is not pure is a falsehood

links.note: Naladiyar 68 grants that the worthy of standing (சீர்கொண்ட சான்றோர்) feel anger and says it cools of itself; the line says that a man of great standing (சீர்) being without anger is false.
links.teaches: Together they move the virtue of the eminent from having no anger to letting anger subside, since one says such a man will feel it and the other says how his anger differs from the low man's.
links.list_adds: Set beside the drunkard's lapses and the greedy judge, it counts anger as a thing that comes with high standing as surely as lapse comes with drink, a turn the quatrain's contrast of the worthy and the low does not make.

links.note: Kural 930 asks whether the drinker, seeing another drunk, does not think of the lapse (சோர்வு) of his own drinking; the line says a drinker without lapse is false.
links.teaches: The couplet hopes the drinker may see his own lapse in another man, and the line states that lapse as certain, so the pair shows the Kural's appeal resting on a fact the drinker refuses: that his lapse is not occasional but sure.
links.list_adds: It makes the drinker's lapse one of ten impossibilities with the greedy judge and the impure ascetic, a type-judgement on a kind of man rather than the couplet's question put to one drinker.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 33 counts as painful the matter of business a drunkard speaks of; the line says a drinker free of lapses is false.
links.teaches: The Innaa line names the pain of dealing with a drinker's affairs and the Muthumozhikkanchi line gives its cause, the lapse that is certain in him, so one reports the effect and the other the reason no business with him is safe.

links.note: Kural 484 says even the world comes to hand (கைகூடும்) if one weighs the time and acts by the place; the line says gain coming to hand (கையுறல்) for one who does not know the time is false.
links.teaches: The couplet makes knowing the time enough for even the greatest gain, and the line makes it necessary for any gain, so together they give timing both halves of a condition: without it nothing comes to hand, with it even the world can.
links.list_adds: It states as an impossibility, beside nine others, the negative half that the couplet's promise leaves unsaid, and drops the couplet's second condition of place.

links.note: Kural 429 says those whose understanding guards against what is coming are not shaken by affliction; the line says one who does not know what is coming cannot guard himself.
links.teaches: The couplet joins knowing and guarding in one phrase and promises calm; the line pulls them apart and makes knowing the prior condition, so the pair shows that the Kural's guarding is itself a kind of knowledge, not a separate defence.
links.list_adds: In a ten that sets each act against the lack that makes it false, it isolates foresight as the single lack that undoes self-protection, where the couplet praises understanding in general.

links.note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration; the line says one who cannot bear lowliness cannot rightly seek greatness.
links.teaches: The couplet describes greatness as bowing once it is had, and the line makes the bearing of low estate the road to it, so together they show humility as both the way to greatness and its mark once reached.
links.list_adds: Paired in its ten with its own mirror (68), it turns the couplet's contrast of two characters into a test of endurance applied to both high and low estate.

links.note: 67 denies greatness to one who cannot bear lowliness; 68 swaps the two words and denies lowliness to one who cannot bear greatness.
links.teaches: Read as a pair, the two lines make the capacity to bear one's station, high or low, the single condition of moving between them, so neither ambition nor humility is genuine in one who cannot endure the other state.

links.note: Kural 541 defines justice as inquiry, no favour to anyone, holding to the ruler's part and acting after thought; the line says justice done by one who craves wealth is false.
links.teaches: The couplet's definition is a procedure and says nothing of the judge's appetites; the line adds a condition on the judge himself, so the pair shows that the four steps can be kept in form and still be false if greed sits behind them.
links.list_adds: It sets greed for wealth among ten lacks that falsify an act, so justice is judged by the character of the one who does it, not by the steps the couplet lists.

links.note: Kural 262 says penance comes to those who have penance and is futile for those without it; the line says penance done by one who is not pure is false.
links.teaches: The couplet's condition for penance is circular, penance belongs to those who already have it, and the line names what that prior possession is, purity, so the pair turns the Kural's riddle into a stated precondition.
links.list_adds: In a ten that names the one lack that falsifies each act, it gives the precondition of penance a name, வாலியன், where the couplet leaves it as penance itself.

links.note: Thirikadugam 80 counts penance taken up by one without restraint of heart (நிறை) as seed sown on scrub; the line says penance by one who is not pure (வாலியன்) is false.
links.teaches: The two name different lacks, restraint of heart and purity, that make penance void, and one calls it barren where the other calls it false, so together they show the penance of the unfit failing both as fruit and as truth.

source_issues: 61 line 2: the core text has a repaired misprint (பேரறவி read பேரறிவி, as tamilvu), and the site's text lacks this line; the reading follows the repaired line.
62: பெருஞ்சீர் ஒன்றன் is doubtful as printed; the pattern of the ten wants a person-noun such as பெருஞ்சீரோன், and the reading assumes it.
